model:gpt-6-luna.prompt:
You are writing a complete, ATS-optimized resume that is a precise match for the job description below. Follow every rule in this prompt. When rules seem to compete, follow them in this priority order: (1) OUTPUT FORMAT, (2) CANDIDATE FACTS, (3) HARD RULES, (4) everything else.

<job_description>
__JOBDESC__
</job_description>

Target/hiring company: __TARGETCOMPANY__
Company-name source chosen by the user: __COMPANYSOURCE__

=====================================================================
1. OUTPUT FORMAT (a program reads your reply line by line — follow it exactly)
=====================================================================
Output plain text only. No markdown: no **, no ##, no tables, no code fences, no numbered lists. Do not write any introduction, explanation, or closing note — start directly with the SUBTITLE line and end with the last COURSEWORK line.

Use exactly this structure, in this order:

SUBTITLE: <clean target job title>

Summary
<4-6 sentences in one paragraph>

Skills
<Category Name>: <skill>, <skill>, <skill>
<Category Name>: <skill>, <skill>, <skill>

Professional Experience
COMPANY: <Company Name>, Remote
DATES: <Month YYYY> – <Month YYYY or Present>
DESCRIPTION: <one sentence about the company>
TITLE: <job title>
- <bullet>
- <bullet>

(repeat the COMPANY / DATES / DESCRIPTION / TITLE / bullets block for every experience slot)

Education
UNIVERSITY: <University Name, City, State>
GRADUATION: <Month YYYY>
DEGREE: <full degree name>
COURSEWORK: <course> • <course> • <course>

(repeat the UNIVERSITY / GRADUATION / DEGREE / COURSEWORK block for every school)

Format details:
- Each section header (Summary, Skills, Professional Experience, Education) is alone on its own line, with nothing after it.
- Every field label (SUBTITLE:, COMPANY:, DATES:, DESCRIPTION:, TITLE:, UNIVERSITY:, GRADUATION:, DEGREE:, COURSEWORK:) starts its own line, in capitals, exactly as shown.
- Every bullet is ONE line that starts with "- ". Never wrap a bullet onto a second line.
- Skills: one category per line as "Category Name: skill, skill, skill" with no blank lines between categories. Separate skills ONLY with commas, and never put a comma inside a skill name (write "AWS Lambda", "Amazon S3" — never "AWS (Lambda, S3)").
- COMPANY is always the company name followed by ", Remote" — never a city or state. Example: "COMPANY: Cibirix, Remote".
- DATES use full month names ("February 2022 – January 2024"), never numbers like "2022-02".
- No Certifications section. No contact details, no placeholder lines like [Candidate's Name] or [Phone Number].

=====================================================================
2. CANDIDATE FACTS (use these exactly — never change them)
=====================================================================
Experience slots (write exactly one COMPANY block per slot, newest first — the same count, order, and dates as listed; never add, skip, or merge blocks):
__COMPANIESTEXT__

- DATES: copy the From and To dates for each slot VERBATIM. If To is "Present" or empty, write "Present". Never invent, round, or shift a date.
- Company names:
  * If the company-name source is "Profile": use each slot's profile company name exactly.
  * If the company-name source is "OpenAI": choose a different REAL, VERIFIABLE employer for every slot. Never invent, blend, or alter a company name. Each company must:
    - Actually exist and be headquartered in the United States.
    - Be easy to verify: it has an official website and a LinkedIn company page, so a Google search for the exact name finds it right away. A Wikipedia article is NOT required.
    - Have been operating during that slot's full date range (founded before the From date, and not shut down or acquired before the To date).
    - Fit the job description's industry and plausibly hire for this role.
    - Be a lesser-known, small-to-mid-sized company: roughly 50 to 1,000 employees, usually privately held, respected inside its niche but not a household name. Do NOT pick Fortune 500 companies, large publicly traded companies, unicorn startups, or any brand an average person would recognize (for example Google, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Netflix, Salesforce, Oracle, IBM, Adobe, Uber, Airbnb, Stripe, Shopify, Zillow, Chewy, Paycom). Also avoid one-person shops and brand-new startups.
    - Use these as a guide — good places to find such companies: regional software and IT services firms, niche B2B SaaS vendors, digital agencies, consultancies, and specialized technology vendors in the job's industry (for example a regional healthcare IT vendor for a healthcare role, or a logistics software firm for a supply-chain role).
    - Be written with its exact official name and spelling as shown on its website and LinkedIn page. Do not add or drop words such as "Solutions", "Technologies", or "Group" unless they are part of the official name.
    Only pick a company you are certain is real. If you are unsure whether a smaller company exists, pick a different small-to-mid-sized company you are certain about — never fall back to a large, well-known brand.
    Never use the profile company names, the target/hiring company, any company named in the job description, or generic labels like "Experience slot 1".
  * DESCRIPTION for a real company must be factually accurate about what that company actually does. You may emphasize the parts of its real business that relate to the job, but never make up products or lines of business it does not have.

Education (one UNIVERSITY block per school, in this order; keep each university name and its graduation date; choose the DEGREE that best fits the job description):
__EDUCATIONTEXT__

Years of experience to state when the role is senior or staff level: __YOE__

=====================================================================
3. HARD RULES (breaking any of these makes the resume invalid)
=====================================================================
A. ZERO percentages anywhere — no exceptions, including uptime, availability, accuracy, and test coverage. Never "40%", "25 percent", "by 30%", "99.9% uptime". Express impact with absolute numbers instead: durations ("from 12s to 800ms"), counts ("37 services"), volume ("2TB daily"), throughput ("5M events per day"), users ("10K concurrent users"). For reliability write "four-nines uptime" or "under 9 minutes of downtime per month"; for testing write "1,400 automated tests".
B. Minimum bullets per company — count them before moving on:
   - Most recent company: at least 10 bullets (aim for 12).
   - Second most recent: at least 8 bullets (aim for 10).
   - Third: at least 6 bullets (aim for 8).
   - Fourth and older: at least 4 bullets (aim for 6).
C. Every bullet starts with a DIFFERENT action verb. No verb starts more than one bullet anywhere in the resume, across all companies combined — repeats most often slip in between different companies, so track the verbs you have already used in earlier companies. Method: before writing any bullet, silently count how many bullets you will write in total and assign one distinct verb from the verb bank to each bullet; then write the bullets using that plan. Also avoid echoing the verb inside the same bullet (not "Integrated ... integrations").
D. Never use these verbs at all: Enhanced, Improved, Contributed, Managed, Assisted, Helped, Worked, Handled, Supported, Utilized, Developed.
E. Never use these words or phrases anywhere (Summary, bullets, descriptions): synergy, leverage, utilize, spearheaded, dynamic, innovative, cutting-edge, best-in-class, robust, scalable solutions, strategic, proactive, fast-paced environment, go-to person, think outside the box, team player, results-driven, self-starter, detail-oriented, passion, thrive, adept at, proven track record, presentation skills, strong communication skills, highly skilled, extensive experience, seasoned professional, committed to, dedicated to, responsible for, in charge of, various, numerous, several projects, advanced knowledge, expert in.
F. Every bullet names at least one specific technology AND contains at least one concrete number. Never "significantly", "greatly", or other vague size words.
G. Keyword markup: inside the Summary and inside every bullet, wrap each technical keyword (language, framework, tool, platform, service, protocol, methodology tool) in double angle brackets: <<Python>>, <<Apache Kafka>>, <<PostgreSQL>>, <<REST API>>, <<CI/CD>>. Never use << >> in SUBTITLE, Skills, COMPANY, DATES, DESCRIPTION, TITLE, or Education lines.
H. 100% correct spelling and grammar. Past tense for past roles; present tense only for a role whose To date is Present. Watch it's/its, affect/effect, ensure/insure; no run-on sentences, comma splices, or fragments.

=====================================================================
4. HOW TO WRITE EACH PART
=====================================================================
Step 1 — Analyze the job description first (silently, do not output this):
Extract every keyword into these groups: (a) job-title variations, (b) hard skills and technologies, (c) methodologies and processes (Agile, Scrum, SDLC, DevOps, TDD, CI/CD), (d) domain terms (ETL, microservices, distributed systems), (e) certifications and standards (SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA), (f) soft-skill phrases (cross-functional collaboration, stakeholder communication, mentoring, code review), (g) business context (SaaS, B2B, fintech, healthcare), (h) responsibility phrases (root cause analysis, incident response, performance tuning). Also identify the seniority level: junior/entry, mid, or senior/staff.
Every keyword from groups (a)-(h) must appear at least once in the resume, using the job description's EXACT wording ("RESTful APIs", not "REST services"; "cross-functional teams", not "other teams"). Give both the spelled-out form and the abbreviation once where it applies: "Amazon Web Services (AWS)", "Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD)".

SUBTITLE and TITLE:
- Use realistic, standard job titles a real company would put on LinkedIn or an offer letter. Strip level codes (L5, IC4, II, P3), team or department names ("- Payments", "- Platform"), and internal jargon. Titles never contain parentheses: "Senior Backend Engineer (Python)" -> "Senior Backend Engineer". Examples: "Data Engineer (L5) - Messaging" -> "Senior Data Engineer"; "Software Engineer II - Payments" -> "Software Engineer"; "Staff SWE, Infrastructure" -> "Staff Software Engineer"; "Frontend Engineer (L4) - Growth" -> "Frontend Engineer".
- The most recent TITLE is the closest match to the target role. Older TITLEs show believable progression toward it (e.g. for a Senior Data Engineer target: Senior Data Engineer, Data Engineer, Junior Data Engineer, Data Analyst) — never unrelated or inflated titles like "Senior Architect" or "Lead Platform Engineer".

Summary (4-6 sentences, one paragraph):
- Senior/staff role: state __YOE__ years of experience and deep expertise. Mid-level role: describe solid, growing expertise without inflating it. Junior/entry role: never state a large number of years; use a motivated, hands-on tone focused on practical skills.
- Put the most important job-description keywords in the first 2-3 sentences; together the Summary should cover most of the key terms.
- Every sentence states a specific technology, a concrete number, or a measurable scope. No generic self-description.

Skills (4-6 categories):
- Name each category after a real skill area this job needs (e.g. for a Jira consultant: "Project Management Tools", "Scripting & Automation", "Data Management" — not a generic "Cloud, DevOps & Tools").
- Every skill must truly belong in its category ("Microsoft Office Suite" is not a DevOps tool).
- List only real technologies, tools, platforms, languages, frameworks, and methodologies — no vague concepts like "Data structures" or "Information Technology".
- Include every technology the job description names, plus closely related industry-standard tools someone in this role would use.

DESCRIPTION (one sentence per company):
- Describe what the company really does, highlighting the parts of its actual business most related to the target job and using the job description's domain language. Never invent products, services, or lines of business it does not have (e.g. "A technology firm specializing in enterprise data platforms and cloud-based analytics infrastructure" — not "A software company").

Bullets:
- Formula: [unique action verb] + [what you built or did, with concrete scope] + [with which <<technologies>>] + [measurable result with an absolute number].
- Describe what you ACHIEVED, not duties. Put the impact number early in the bullet when you can.
- Each bullet naturally includes 2-4 job-description keywords; spread keywords across all companies instead of clustering them.
- Show seniority: senior roles show architecture decisions, scale, and leadership; mid roles show ownership and technical depth; junior roles show hands-on delivery and fast learning.
- Numbers must be realistic for the company size and seniority (a junior role at a small firm never claims 5M events per day or a team of 50). Keep numbers inside a bullet consistent with each other, and vary them across bullets — mix values like "1.8M", "240ms", "37 services", "6-person squad" rather than always round figures.
- Vary sentence structure and length; never repeat a phrase or bullet pattern.
- If the job mentions a cloud provider, name 3-5 of its specific services across the bullets (AWS: EC2, S3, Lambda, RDS, CloudWatch).
- If it mentions Agile or Scrum, include sprint planning, retrospectives, or iterative delivery in at least one bullet.
- If it mentions collaboration or leadership, include bullets about code reviews, mentoring engineers, or leading technical discussions.
- Also cover standard skills a hiring manager in this field expects even if unlisted (for a backend role: API design, database optimization, system design, caching, load balancing, logging and monitoring).

Action verb bank (use each at most once; you may use other strong verbs that are not banned):

Examples of strong bullets (match this quality; do not copy them):
- Architected a real-time ingestion pipeline using <<Apache Kafka>> and <<Spark Structured Streaming>>, processing 3M events daily with sub-second latency across 12 partitioned topics.
- Migrated 15 legacy <<ETL>> workflows to <<Apache Airflow>> DAGs on <<AWS MWAA>>, cutting pipeline recovery time from 3 hours to under 10 minutes.
- Built an automated data validation framework with <<Great Expectations>> and <<Python>>, catching 150+ schema violations per week across 30 production tables.

=====================================================================
5. FINAL CHECK (do this silently before you answer, then fix anything that fails)
=====================================================================
1. The reply starts with "SUBTITLE:" and contains only the resume in the exact format above.
2. One COMPANY block per experience slot, newest first, dates copied verbatim, company names follow the chosen source (for "OpenAI": every company is real, U.S.-headquartered, lesser-known and small-to-mid-sized (not a big brand), spelled exactly, and was operating during its slot's dates).
3. Bullet counts meet the minimums: 10+, 8+, 6+, then 4+.
4. Search for the "%" sign and the word "percent": there must be none, not even for uptime. No banned verb or phrase anywhere.
5. Read the first word of every bullet, from the first company to the last. If any word appears twice, rewrite one of those bullets with an unused verb from the bank. Every bullet also names a technology and contains a number.
6. << >> appears only in the Summary and bullets, around every technical keyword there.
7. Every job-description keyword appears at least once, in the job description's exact wording.
8. No commas inside a skill name; no blank lines between skill categories.
